stem: A product listing page (a client-rendered React SPA) takes about 6 seconds to show its hero on a mid-range phone. Lighthouse reports LCP at 5.8 s. The single JavaScript bundle is 1.9 MB, and the LCP element is a 2400 px wide JPEG hero marked `loading="lazy"`. Which two changes go after the biggest costs first? (Choose two.)

options.text: Drop `loading="lazy"` from the above-the-fold hero, serve it at the rendered size in a modern format with `srcset`, and consider `fetchpriority="high"`
options.why: Lazy-loading the LCP image delays its request, and a 2400 px JPEG on a phone wastes bytes. Both push LCP out directly.

options.text: Run a bundle analyser, split the code by route with dynamic `import()` / `React.lazy`, and replace or trim the heaviest dependencies
options.why: A client-rendered page cannot paint content until its JavaScript downloads, parses and runs, so a 1.9 MB bundle is on the critical path.

options.text: Wrap every component in `React.memo` so the page renders fewer times during load
options.why: Memoisation reduces re-render work after load. The first render still happens, and none of the download cost changes.

options.text: Add `loading="lazy"` to every image on the page, including the hero, so fewer bytes compete with the bundle
options.why: Lazy-loading the hero is part of the problem: the browser waits for layout before it even starts fetching the LCP image.

options.text: Swap the data-fetching `useEffect` calls for `useLayoutEffect` so data arrives before the first paint
options.why: Layout effects block paint; they do not make the network faster. The page would paint later, not sooner.

explanation: Interviewers who ask "the page is slow, how do you debug it?" want a measured order of attack: look at the Network panel and Lighthouse, find the LCP element, and see what is on the critical path. For a client-rendered app that is usually the JavaScript bundle (fix with analysis, route-level splitting and lighter dependencies) and the hero image (correct size, modern format, no lazy loading above the fold, higher fetch priority). A CDN with good cache headers helps both. Re-render tuning such as `memo` comes later because it does not touch load cost.
reference: web.dev: Optimize Largest Contentful Paint; react.dev: lazy

stem: On a landing page, the hero image is the largest element in the viewport. A CDN misconfiguration makes that image arrive 3 seconds later than before. The text, layout and the hero's reserved box (fixed `width` and `height`) still appear on time, and the page responds to taps as before. Which Core Web Vital gets noticeably worse?

options.text: Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS)
options.why: The hero box already has reserved dimensions, so nothing moves when the image finally arrives.

options.text: Largest Contentful Paint (LCP)
options.why: LCP is the time at which the largest image or text block in the viewport is rendered, so a late hero image delays it directly.

options.text: Interaction to Next Paint (INP)
options.why: INP measures how quickly the page responds to user input, and the stem says taps respond as before.

options.text: Time to First Byte (TTFB)
options.why: TTFB measures the response for the HTML document itself, not for images loaded afterwards.

explanation: Each Core Web Vital measures one thing. LCP is loading: when the largest content element paints. CLS is visual stability: how much content jumps. INP is responsiveness to input. A late hero image hits LCP. If the image had no reserved size it would also cause CLS when it popped in, which is why interviewers often follow up with "and how do you stop the jump?" (set dimensions or `aspect-ratio`).

stem:
You are choosing a rendering strategy for three parts of one product:

1. A logged-in analytics dashboard with per-user data, no SEO needs, refreshed by polling.
2. Product pages that must rank in search, with prices and stock that change several times an hour.
3. A marketing blog whose posts rarely change after publishing.

Which assignment fits best?

options.text: Dashboard: SSG. Product pages: CSR. Blog: SSR on every request
options.why: Per-user dashboard data cannot be built once at deploy time, and client-only product pages weaken first paint and SEO, the two things those pages need.

options.text: Dashboard: SSR. Product pages: SSG built once per deploy. Blog: CSR
options.why: Product prices would stay stale until the next deploy, and a client-rendered blog gives up SEO for content that is easy to pre-render.

options.text: Dashboard: CSR. Product pages: SSR or ISR. Blog: SSG
options.why: Each part gets what it needs: rich client interactivity behind login, fresh and crawlable product HTML, and cheap pre-built pages for static posts.

options.text: Everything SSG, with a client-side refetch on mount to update stale data
options.why: A build cannot produce per-user dashboards, and pages that show stale prices until JavaScript runs give crawlers and first paint the wrong data.

explanation: The interviewer wants to hear the trade-offs, not a favourite. CSR suits private, highly interactive screens where SEO does not matter. SSR builds HTML per request, so content is fresh and crawlable at the cost of server work on every hit. SSG builds HTML once and serves it from a CDN, which is ideal for content that rarely changes. ISR sits between them: static pages that regenerate after a time window or on demand. Most real apps mix all of these per route.

stem: An interviewer asks why server-side rendering helps first paint and SEO compared with a client-rendered SPA. Which two statements are accurate? (Choose two.)

options.text: The first HTML response already contains the page content, so users and crawlers see it before any JavaScript has downloaded
options.why: With CSR the first response is a near-empty shell, and content only appears after the bundle runs and fetches data.

options.text: With SSR the page ships no JavaScript for its interactive components, because the server already rendered them
options.why: Interactive components still ship their JavaScript. SSR adds HTML up front; it does not remove the client bundle.

options.text: An SSR page can look ready before it is interactive: buttons do nothing until the JavaScript loads and hydrates them
options.why: Hydration attaches event handlers to the server HTML, so there is a window where content is visible but not yet interactive.

options.text: SSR always gives a lower Time to First Byte than serving a pre-built static page from a CDN
options.why: Rendering on each request adds server work, so SSR usually has a higher TTFB than static HTML from a CDN edge.

options.text: Search engines cannot index client-rendered pages at all, so SSR is the only way to appear in results
options.why: Google can render JavaScript, but rendering is deferred and less reliable, and many other crawlers and link previews do not run it. SSR is safer, not the only way.

explanation: SSR moves the first render to the server. The user gets meaningful HTML immediately, which helps FCP and LCP, and crawlers and social previews get real content. The cost is server work per request, and a gap between "visible" and "interactive" until hydration finishes. A good answer mentions both sides, and that static generation gives the same SEO benefit with lower TTFB when the content does not change per request.
reference: react.dev: hydrateRoot; Next.js docs: Server and Client Components

stem: A high-traffic marketing page is server-rendered on every request. Its content comes from a CMS and changes about once a day. Server costs spike during campaigns. The page must stay crawlable and should show the new content within a few hours of an edit, without anyone redeploying. What should the team do?

options.text: Switch the page to client-side rendering so the server only sends a small HTML shell
options.why: It cuts server work but sends crawlers and users an empty shell first, which hurts SEO and first paint.

options.text: Generate it statically and regenerate it on a timer or when the CMS publishes (ISR / on-demand revalidation)
options.why: The CDN serves cached HTML to almost every visitor, and the page is rebuilt in the background when it goes stale or when an edit happens.

options.text: Keep SSR on every request, but wrap the page components in `React.memo` so that each server render does less work
options.why: `memo` skips re-renders inside one React tree. Each new request is a fresh render on the server, so it saves nothing here.

options.text: Generate the page once at build time and redeploy when content changes
options.why: This works only if someone redeploys after each edit, which the requirement rules out.

explanation: When content changes rarely but must stay fresh without redeploys, Incremental Static Regeneration (or on-demand revalidation from a CMS webhook) gives the CDN-speed and SEO of static HTML with bounded staleness. Interviewers use this to check you know ISR exists and when plain SSR is wasted work.

stem: You are asked what Babel, Webpack and Vite each do in a React project. Which two statements are correct? (Choose two.)

options.text: Babel transforms source code, for example JSX into function calls and newer syntax into older syntax; it does not bundle modules together
options.why: Babel is a compiler working file by file. Combining modules into bundles is the bundler's job.

options.text: Webpack understands JSX by itself, so a React project does not need a loader such as `babel-loader` or `swc-loader`
options.why: Webpack only understands JavaScript and JSON out of the box. JSX needs a loader to transform it first.

options.text: In development, Vite serves source files to the browser as native ES modules and transforms each one on request, so start-up does not wait for a full bundle
options.why: That is why a Vite dev server starts quickly even in large projects: only the modules the page imports are processed.

options.text: Vite's production build is done by Webpack, with Vite adding only the dev server on top
options.why: Vite does its production build with its own Rollup-based pipeline (Rolldown in recent versions), not Webpack.

options.text: Tree shaking works equally well on CommonJS `require` calls and on ES `import` statements
options.why: Tree shaking relies on the static structure of ES modules. CommonJS exports are decided at runtime, so bundlers mostly cannot prune them.

explanation: A clear answer separates the jobs. A transpiler (Babel, SWC, esbuild) rewrites syntax. A bundler (Webpack, Rollup, Rolldown) follows imports, builds the dependency graph, splits chunks and removes dead code. Vite is a build tool that skips bundling in development, serving native ES modules, and bundles for production. Interviewers usually follow up with "why is Vite's dev server faster?" or "why does tree shaking need ES modules?".

options.text: Tree shaking only runs on named imports; default and namespace imports are always bundled in full
options.why: Bundlers can tree-shake a namespace import when its property accesses are static. The difference here is the module format.

options.text: `require` loads modules synchronously, so the bundler must include them eagerly, whereas `import` loads them lazily at runtime
options.why: Static `import` is not lazy; it is bundled too. Only dynamic `import()` creates a separate chunk.

options.text: CommonJS exports are assembled at runtime, so unused ones cannot be proven dead; ES `import`/`export` are static
options.why: Tree shaking needs to know at build time which exports are referenced, and only static ES module syntax gives it that.

options.text: The lodash package is minified as one file, so it cannot be split, while lodash-es is split into separate files per function
options.why: File layout alone is not what decides it. A bundler can drop unused exports from one ES module file, but cannot do the same for a CommonJS module.

explanation: Tree shaking is dead-code elimination based on the static import/export graph. ES modules declare imports and exports at the top level with fixed names, so a bundler can mark what is used and drop the rest (helped by `"sideEffects": false` in package.json). CommonJS assigns to `module.exports` at runtime, so in general the whole module must be kept. This is the standard follow-up when candidates mention tree shaking.

stem: In a frontend system design round you are designing a WhatsApp Web-style chat: messages and typing indicators must flow both ways with low latency, and the server must push new messages the moment they arrive. Which transport fits best?

options.text: Server-Sent Events, with the browser sending typing indicators back through the same event stream
options.why: SSE is a one-way server-to-client stream. Anything the client sends needs separate HTTP requests.

options.text: HTTP polling every two seconds for new messages, with a POST for each message sent
options.why: Polling adds up to two seconds of delay and many empty requests, which is poor for real-time chat at scale.

options.text: A WebSocket connection carrying both directions over one long-lived channel
options.why: WebSockets are full-duplex: either side can send at any time with little overhead per message, which suits chat and typing indicators.

options.text: A service worker that intercepts `fetch` calls and returns new messages from its cache
options.why: A service worker proxies the page's own requests. It does not open a live channel to receive the server's pushes.

explanation: The interviewer wants to see that you match the transport to the data flow. WebSockets suit two-way, low-latency traffic such as chat, presence and multiplayer. Server-Sent Events suit one-way server pushes such as notifications, live scores or streaming an AI response, and they reconnect automatically. Long polling is a fallback when neither is available. A complete answer also covers reconnecting and fetching missed messages.

stem: Your chat client's WebSocket drops when users switch networks. When the server restarts, thousands of clients reconnect at once and overload it. Which reconnect strategy meets all of these: it does not stampede the server, it recovers quickly after a short blip, and it does not lose messages sent while offline?

options.text: On `close`, reconnect immediately in a loop until it succeeds, then carry on from the next message the server pushes
options.why: Instant retries from every client hammer a recovering server, and messages sent while the client was disconnected are never fetched.

options.text: Retry with exponential backoff plus random jitter and a cap, reset the delay after a successful `open`, then request messages since the last ID the client saw
options.why: Jitter spreads the reconnects out, the backoff protects the server, the reset keeps short blips fast, and the "since last ID" sync fills the gap.

options.text: Retry every 5 seconds forever, and reload the whole page once the socket opens so the history is fresh
options.why: Every client still retries in lock-step on the same schedule, and a full reload throws away drafts and scroll position.

options.text: Avoid reconnects altogether by sending a heartbeat ping every 100 ms to keep the socket alive, and rely on the server to replay anything the client missed
options.why: Heartbeats detect dead connections; they cannot prevent network changes. Very frequent pings also waste battery and bandwidth.

explanation: Reconnect logic is a classic chat follow-up. Exponential backoff (1 s, 2 s, 4 s… up to a cap) with jitter avoids a thundering herd. Resetting the counter after a good connection keeps recovery fast. Correctness needs a resync step: the client remembers the last message ID or cursor it saw and asks for everything after it, so nothing sent during the outage is lost. Heartbeats are worth mentioning, but for detecting half-open connections.

stem: Messages are stored normalised: `byId` maps IDs to messages and `order` lists IDs. When the user sends a message it should appear at once as "sending…". The server later broadcasts the saved message (with its real ID) back to every client, including the sender. Some users see their own message twice. Which design fixes this?

options.text: Do not add the message locally; wait for the server broadcast and show it then
options.why: This avoids duplicates but drops the optimistic "appears at once" requirement, so the chat feels laggy.

options.text: When a broadcast arrives, skip it whenever a message with the same text from the same sender is already somewhere in the list
options.why: Users often send the same text twice ("ok", "👍"), so text matching drops real messages.

options.text: Send a client-generated ID with each pending message; when the broadcast echoes it back, replace the pending entry
options.why: The client ID links the optimistic entry to its saved copy, so the pending entry is swapped in place and never duplicated.

options.text: Append the broadcast as usual, and filter duplicates during render by comparing timestamps
options.why: The client and server clocks differ, so timestamps do not match reliably, and filtering on every render hides the bug instead of fixing the state.

explanation: Optimistic sends need a way to reconcile the local copy with the server copy. The usual pattern is a client-generated ID (for example `crypto.randomUUID()`) stored on the pending message and echoed back by the server. On the echo you replace the entry, keyed by that ID, and set its status to sent; on failure you mark it failed with a retry button. Interviewers are checking that you have thought past the "happy path".

stem: A news feed uses infinite scroll. While the user is reading post 40, a WebSocket delivers 3 new posts that belong at the top. Which approach gives the best experience?

options.text: Prepend the new posts to the list as soon as they arrive
options.why: Inserting content above the reader shifts everything down, so the post they were reading jumps out of view.

options.text: Refetch the first page and replace the list with it
options.why: The user loses their place and every page loaded below, and scroll position jumps back to the top.

options.text: Hold the new posts aside and show a "3 new posts" pill; tapping it prepends them and scrolls to the top
options.why: The reader keeps their position, and the new content is one tap away when they want it.

options.text: Ignore the real-time posts and show the new ones only after the user pulls to refresh or reloads the whole page
options.why: This is stable but throws away the real-time requirement; a refresh also loses scroll position and loaded pages.

explanation: Feed design questions probe whether you protect the user's reading position. Buffering live items behind a "new posts" banner (as most social apps do) avoids layout jumps. It also works well with cursor-based pagination: older pages keep loading from the bottom cursor while new items wait in a separate buffer at the top.

stem: After scrolling through about 2,000 posts, a news feed becomes janky, and images popping in make the page jump. Posts have variable heights (text, images, videos). Which two changes address these problems? (Choose two.)

options.text: Virtualise the list so only the posts in and near the viewport are mounted, measuring each row's real height as it renders
options.why: This keeps the DOM small however far the user scrolls. Variable-height rows need measurement, which libraries such as TanStack Virtual handle.

options.text: Wrap every post in `React.memo`; once posts stop re-rendering, the number of DOM nodes no longer matters
options.why: `memo` cuts re-render work, but 2,000 mounted posts still cost memory, layout and style work on every scroll.

options.text: Reserve each image's space up front with known `width`/`height` or `aspect-ratio` from the API
options.why: Reserved space stops the jumps, and it also lets the virtualiser estimate row heights before the media loads.

options.text: Use the array index as each post's `key` so React can reuse DOM nodes while scrolling
options.why: Index keys break state and focus when items are inserted or removed; they do not reduce the number of nodes.

options.text: Load every page up front on first visit so scrolling never waits for the network
options.why: This makes the first load much slower and makes the DOM-size problem worse.

explanation: Long feeds hit two separate problems. DOM size: thousands of mounted nodes slow down layout, style and memory, and the fix is windowing (overscan a few rows; measure variable heights). Layout shift: media without reserved space moves content when it loads, and the fix is dimensions or `aspect-ratio` from the API. Interviewers like candidates who name both and do not reach for `memo` by reflex.
reference: web.dev: Virtualize large lists with react-window

stem: A feed stores posts in state, and tapping Like must update the count instantly. If the request fails, only that post should revert, even if the user liked other posts in the meantime. Given `const flip = (p) => ({ ...p, liked: !p.liked, likes: p.likes + (p.liked ? -1 : 1) });`, which handler meets every requirement?

options.why: Both the optimistic change and the rollback are functional updates aimed at one post, so changes to other posts made in between survive.
Restoring the whole snapshot also undoes every other like or newly loaded page that happened while this request was in flight.
It mutates state and passes the same array back, so React bails out and nothing re-renders; there is no rollback either.
Correct and safe, but not optimistic: the count changes only after the round trip, which fails the "instantly" requirement.

explanation: An optimistic update should be undone the same way it was applied: as a targeted change to the latest state, not by restoring an old snapshot. Snapshots are only safe when nothing else can change in between, which is rarely true in a feed. Libraries such as TanStack Query or React 19's `useOptimistic` package this pattern, but interviewers want to see that you can reason about it by hand.

options.text: `A b`
options.why: That is what a correct implementation logs. This `setState` does not write to slot 0.

options.text: `a b`
options.why: `setState` reads `cursor` when it is called, and by then the cursor is 2, so `'A'` goes into an unused slot and `a` is unchanged.

options.text: `a A`
options.why: The write does not land in slot 1. The cursor was 2 after the first render, not 1.

options.text: `a undefined`
options.why: Both slots 0 and 1 were initialised in the first render, and the stray write went to slot 2, so neither read is `undefined`.

explanation: The bug is that `setState` uses the shared `cursor` variable instead of capturing its own slot index (`const i = cursor++` and then `hooks[i] = next`). This is the heart of the "how are hooks stored?" question: React keeps each component's hooks in call order (a linked list on the fiber), and each setter is bound to its own slot. Because slots are matched purely by position, the call order must be identical on every render.
reference: react.dev: Rules of Hooks; react.dev: State as a Snapshot

stem: A component needs an `age` state only when `showAge` is true, so someone wrote `if (showAge) { const [age, setAge] = useState(0); }`. Which two rewrites follow the Rules of Hooks? (Choose two.)

options.text: Call `useState(0)` unconditionally at the top level, and use `age` only when `showAge` is true
options.why: The hook now runs in the same position on every render; the condition only decides how its value is used.

options.text: Keep the `if`, but wrap the `useState` call in `try/catch` so a hook-order error cannot crash the component
options.why: The problem is not an exception in that call; skipping it shifts the slots of every later hook. A `try/catch` changes nothing about that.

options.text: Move the age field into its own `<AgeField />` component that calls `useState`, and render it with `{showAge && <AgeField />}`
options.why: The child has its own fiber and its own list of hooks, so mounting it conditionally is fine. Its state resets when it unmounts.

options.text: Call it inside `useMemo(() => useState(0), [showAge])` so it only runs when `showAge` changes
options.why: Hooks cannot be called inside callbacks passed to other hooks, and this would still run a variable number of hooks.

options.text: Give the call a unique key, such as `useState(0, 'age')`, so React matches it by name instead of order
options.why: `useState` has no key parameter. React matches hooks only by call order.

explanation: Since hooks are matched by position, the fix is always to make the call order fixed: call the hook every time and branch on its value, or push the conditional part into a child component that owns its own hooks. React 19's `use` is the one exception that may be called conditionally, because it does not occupy a state slot in the same way.

stem: In React 19, which two of these calls are allowed by the Rules of Hooks? (Choose two.)

options.text: `useState` called inside `items.forEach(...)` in the component body, once per item in a list that can grow
options.why: The number of hook calls would change with the list length, which shifts every later slot. Each item needs its own component.

options.text: `use(ThemeContext)` called inside an `if (isDark) { … }` block in the component body
options.why: `use` is the documented exception: it can be called inside conditions and loops, unlike `useContext`.

options.text: `useEffect` called inside an `onClick` handler so the effect only starts after the first click
options.why: Hooks must run during render. Event handlers run later and outside React's render, so this throws.

options.text: A custom hook `useCart()` that calls `useReducer` and `useEffect` at its own top level, itself called at the top level of a component
options.why: Custom hooks may call other hooks at their top level; their hooks simply occupy slots in the calling component.

options.text: An early `return null` placed before a `useState` call when the user is logged out
options.why: On renders that return early, the later hook is skipped, so the hook count changes between renders.

explanation: The rule is "same hooks, same order, every render": only call hooks at the top level of components and custom hooks, never in conditions, loops, nested functions, event handlers or after an early return. `use` is special because it reads a promise or context without holding a state slot. Interviewers use variations of this to check that you understand the reason for the rule rather than just the lint error.
reference: react.dev: Rules of Hooks; react.dev: use

stem: You maintain a design-system `Button`. Consumers need to pick a `variant` and `size`, add their own spacing class (`className="mt-4"`), and pass any native button prop such as `type`, `aria-label` or `onClick`. Rendering `<Button variant="danger" className="mt-4" type="submit" aria-label="Delete">Delete</Button>` should produce a single `<button>` that has all of these. Which implementation meets every requirement? (`cx` joins truthy class names.)

options.why: Passing `className` replaces the design-system classes entirely, so the button renders with only `mt-4` and loses its styling.
Only `onClick` and `children` get through, so `type` and `aria-label` are silently dropped.
It merges the consumer's class with the variant classes and forwards every other prop, including `children` and, in React 19, `ref`.
Exposing raw style props drops the variant API entirely, lets every team invent its own colours, and still cannot express hover states.

explanation: A good design-system primitive offers a small set of named variants (so teams stay consistent), merges rather than replaces consumer classes, and passes through native props so accessibility attributes and form behaviour keep working. In React 19 `ref` is a regular prop, so `...rest` forwards it without `forwardRef`. Headless libraries add a slot or `asChild` prop for rendering a link as a button.
reference: react.dev: Passing Props to a Component

stem: Twelve product apps use your shared component library. You need to rename `Button`'s `type` prop (for visual style) to `variant`, and add dark mode without asking each app to pass colours. Which two decisions are sound? (Choose two.)

options.text: Rename the prop in a patch release, because the change is small and every app should upgrade promptly
options.why: Removing a prop breaks consumers. Under semver a breaking change needs a major version, whatever its size.

options.text: Accept both props in a minor release with a development warning for `type`, then remove `type` in the next major version
options.why: This gives teams a non-breaking migration window and keeps semver honest about when the break actually lands.

options.text: Add a `dark` boolean prop to every component and let each component choose its own dark colours
options.why: Every component would need to receive the prop, and colours would drift between components with no single source of truth.

options.text: Define design tokens as CSS custom properties and swap their values under a theme selector such as `[data-theme="dark"]`
options.why: Components read `var(--color-bg)` and friends, so switching the theme changes one attribute instead of re-rendering with new props.

options.text: Let each app fork the library so it can make its own changes without waiting for releases
options.why: Forks remove the consistency the library exists for, and fixes stop flowing back to every app.

explanation: Maintaining a design system is partly an API-versioning problem: deprecate, warn, and remove only in a major release, with a changelog and ideally a codemod. Theming scales best through design tokens published as CSS variables, which work with any styling approach and with Server Components. Interviewers at senior level are listening for this process thinking, not just component code.

stem: You are designing a typeahead that calls a suggestions API. It must keep request volume low, reuse answers for repeated queries, and never show results for an older query than the one in the box. Which two decisions meet those requirements? (Choose two.)

options.text: Cache results in a `Map` keyed by the normalised query (trimmed and lower-cased), with a size limit or TTL
options.why: Normalising the key makes "React " and "react" share a cache entry, and the limit stops the cache growing forever.

options.text: Rely on the debounce to keep responses in order, because only one request can be in flight after a pause
options.why: Debouncing reduces how many requests start, but a slow earlier response can still arrive after a later one.

options.text: Debounce input by roughly 200–300 ms, and drop any response whose query no longer matches the latest one (or abort the earlier request)
options.why: The debounce cuts traffic, and the latest-query check or `AbortController` handles out-of-order responses.

options.text: Key the cache by the full request URL including a timestamp parameter, so each entry is guaranteed fresh
options.why: A timestamp makes every key unique, so the cache never hits.

options.text: Throttle to one request per second, and send the request on every keystroke during that second once the window resets
options.why: Throttling adds lag after the user stops typing, and without a race check the old responses can still win.

explanation: A typeahead design answer usually covers four things: debounce input, cache by normalised query, handle races (latest-request ID, ignore flag or `AbortController`), and accessible combobox markup. Debounce and race handling solve different problems, and interviewers often ask "does debouncing fix the race?" to check you know that.

stem: For the same typeahead, screen-reader users must hear which suggestion is highlighted while they press the arrow keys, and must be able to keep typing at the same time. Which markup pattern fits?

options.text: Keep focus on the `<input role="combobox">` with `aria-expanded` and `aria-controls` pointing to a `role="listbox"`, and set `aria-activedescendant` to the highlighted `role="option"`'s id
options.why: Focus never leaves the input, so typing keeps working, while `aria-activedescendant` tells assistive tech which option is active.

options.text: Render the suggestions as `role="menu"` with `role="menuitem"` children and move focus into the menu on ArrowDown
options.why: Menus are for lists of actions, not for choosing a value, and moving focus out of the input interrupts typing.

options.text: Give every suggestion `tabindex="0"` so users can Tab through them and press Enter to choose
options.why: Tab should leave the widget, not walk through dozens of options; the arrow keys are the expected way to move inside a listbox.

options.text: Put an `aria-label` on the input listing every current suggestion, updated on each keystroke
options.why: This reads out one long label with no notion of a highlighted option, and it changes on every keystroke.

explanation: The WAI-ARIA combobox pattern keeps DOM focus on the text input and uses `aria-activedescendant` to point at the visually highlighted option inside a `listbox`. Each option has an id and `aria-selected` on the active one. Interviewers at senior level often add accessibility to the typeahead design to see whether you know this pattern.

stem: An interviewer asks when you would use a web worker and when a service worker in a React app. Which two statements are correct? (Choose two.)

options.text: Both kinds of worker can read and update the DOM, so a heavy render can be moved off the main thread
options.why: Neither kind has DOM access. They talk to the page by passing messages.

options.text: A web worker runs a script on a background thread and exchanges data with the page through `postMessage`, so it suits CPU-heavy work such as parsing a large file
options.why: The main thread stays free to handle input and render while the worker computes.

options.text: A web worker shares the page's JavaScript variables, so it can read React state directly
options.why: Workers have their own global scope. Data is copied (or transferred) between them, never shared by reference.

options.text: A service worker sits between the page and the network and can intercept `fetch` requests, so it suits offline support, caching strategies and push notifications
options.why: It acts as a programmable network proxy for its scope, which is what makes PWAs work offline.

options.text: A service worker stays running for as long as the site is open, so it is a good place for long calculations
options.why: Browsers stop idle service workers and start them again on events, so long-running work does not belong there.

explanation: Web workers are for computation off the main thread; service workers are for the network layer (caching, offline, background sync, push). Neither can touch the DOM. A strong answer gives an example of each, for example parsing a 50 MB CSV in a web worker, and serving the app shell from a cache-first service worker.
reference: MDN: Using Web Workers; MDN: Service Worker API

stem: A React PWA registers a service worker that serves `index.html` and the JS bundles cache-first. After a deploy, users who already have a tab open keep seeing the old version, even after reloading. What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: The browser still holds the old hashed bundle filenames in memory, and only clearing the browser cache will remove them
options.why: Hashed filenames are what let new bundles load. The issue is that the old cached `index.html` keeps pointing at the old ones.

options.text: Service workers cannot update once installed; users must unregister them in DevTools
options.why: Browsers check for an updated service worker script on navigation. The new one installs but does not take over immediately.

options.text: The old worker keeps controlling the open tabs and serving the cached `index.html`; the new worker waits until those tabs close, unless the app prompts the user and calls `skipWaiting()`
options.why: This is the service worker lifecycle: a new version stays "waiting" while any client is controlled by the old one, and a normal reload does not change that.

options.text: React's production build caches components in `localStorage`, and the old ones are read on start-up
options.why: React does not persist components to `localStorage`; the stale files come from the service worker's cache.

explanation: Update handling is the usual service-worker trap. With cache-first HTML, the old worker serves the old shell, and the new worker sits in the "waiting" state until every tab it would replace is closed. Common fixes: serve the HTML network-first, and show an "Update available" toast that calls `skipWaiting()` and then reloads. Interviewers who ask about PWAs usually probe this lifecycle.

stem: A host app and a remote app are joined with Webpack Module Federation. Components loaded from the remote crash with "Invalid hook call", and the bundle shows two copies of `react`. Which change fixes this?

options.text: Set `eager: true` for `react` in the remote only, so React is in the remote's initial chunk
options.why: `eager` only decides which chunk contains the module. Without sharing it as a singleton, the remote still uses its own copy.

options.text: Wrap every remote component in `<StrictMode>` in the host so hook errors are surfaced and recovered
options.why: StrictMode adds development checks; it cannot merge two React copies.

options.text: In both the host and the remote, list `react` and `react-dom` under `shared` with `singleton: true` and a compatible `requiredVersion`
options.why: Every federated app then resolves the same React instance at runtime, so hooks find the renderer's dispatcher.

options.text: Re-export React from the host as `window.HostReact`, and at build time alias the remote's imports of hooks such as `useState` and `useEffect` to it
options.why: Patching only some imports leaves the remote's other React code on its own copy, and it is fragile across upgrades.

explanation: Module Federation can share dependencies at runtime. React must be shared as a singleton (one instance for the whole page) because hooks, context and the renderer depend on module-level state. `requiredVersion` and `strictVersion` control what happens when versions disagree. Interviewers ask this to see whether you have actually run micro-frontends in production.
reference: webpack docs: ModuleFederationPlugin (shared); react.dev: Invalid Hook Call Warning

stem: Following on from the previous setup: why does a component that imports hooks from a second copy of React fail with "Invalid hook call", even when both copies are the same version?

options.text: React compares its own version string with the renderer's and refuses to run hooks when two copies are loaded
options.why: React does not check versions this way; the error appears with identical versions too.

options.text: Each copy of React schedules its own render pass, so the component is rendered twice and the hook counts no longer match
options.why: The second copy never renders anything; there is only one renderer (the host's `react-dom`).

options.text: The renderer sets the "current hooks dispatcher" on the React instance it imported; hooks from the second copy read that copy's dispatcher, which is never set
options.why: Hooks look up their implementation through module-level state on the `react` package, so a different copy sees nothing and throws.

options.text: The second copy overwrites the global `window.React`, so the host's components lose their hooks and only the remote's work
options.why: Bundled React does not rely on a global variable, and the error is thrown by the remote's hooks, not the host's.

explanation: Hooks are not standalone functions: `useState` forwards to a dispatcher that `react-dom` installs on its own copy of `react` while rendering a component. A component that imports `useState` from another copy reads that copy's empty dispatcher and throws. The same failure appears with `npm link` or a monorepo that installs React twice; `npm ls react` shows it.

stem: A team of six engineers ships one product from one repository. Builds take 8 minutes, and someone proposes splitting the app into micro-frontends to speed things up. What is the soundest response?

options.text: Split by page into separately deployed micro-frontends now, because that is how large companies scale frontends
options.why: It adds runtime integration, shared-dependency versioning and duplicated tooling, all to solve a build-speed problem.

options.text: Put each section in an `<iframe>` served by its own build so they can never conflict
options.why: Iframes isolate well but make routing, shared state, styling and accessibility much harder, for no organisational gain here.

options.text: Publish each feature as a versioned npm package and have the app install the latest of each
options.why: This keeps one deployable but adds release and version coordination across packages, which slows a single team down.

options.text: Keep a modular single app, fix build speed with tooling (caching, a faster bundler, splitting the build), and revisit micro-frontends when several autonomous teams need independent releases
options.why: Micro-frontends pay off in organisational scale. For one small team, their costs exceed their benefits.

explanation: Micro-frontends mainly solve an organisational problem: many teams that need to deploy independently. Their costs include duplicated dependencies, keeping shared libraries like React as singletons, consistent UX across apps, cross-app communication and more complex testing. A staff-level answer explains when not to use them, not just how they work.

stem: In a collaborative document editor, two users type in the same paragraph at the same time. Which two statements about Operational Transformation (OT) and CRDTs are accurate? (Choose two.)

options.text: OT transforms each incoming operation against concurrent ones (for example shifting an insert position), usually with a central server that fixes a single order
options.why: This is how Google Docs-style editors keep both users' edits: positions are adjusted, and the server orders the operations.

options.text: Last-write-wins on the whole document keeps both users' concurrent edits, as long as the clocks are in sync
options.why: The later save overwrites the earlier one, so one user's edit is lost regardless of the clocks.

options.text: CRDTs give each inserted element a unique, ordered identity so replicas converge whatever order they receive operations in, which also suits offline and peer-to-peer editing
options.why: Because merges commute, no central ordering is needed; libraries such as Yjs and Automerge use this.

options.text: CRDTs need a central server to decide the order of every operation before clients apply them
options.why: Not needing a central order is the main point of CRDTs, although a server is often used to relay and store updates.

options.text: Both OT and CRDTs prevent conflicts by locking the paragraph while one user is typing
options.why: Locking is a different, cruder strategy; both OT and CRDTs let users edit concurrently and merge the results.

explanation: Real-time collaboration questions at staff level expect the OT vs CRDT trade-off. OT: compact operations, but it needs a central server and tricky transformation functions. CRDT: convergence without central ordering and good offline support, at the cost of extra metadata. Good answers also mention batching operations, presence (cursors and selections) sent on a separate, lossy channel, and undo per user.

stem: You are designing a Google Sheets-like grid with 10,000 rows and 50 columns. Remote collaborators' edits arrive at about 50 per second. Which design keeps typing and scrolling responsive?

options.text: Render all 500,000 cells in a `<table>`, with each cell wrapped in `React.memo` so only edited cells re-render
options.why: Half a million mounted cells is far too much DOM to lay out and scroll smoothly, whatever `memo` saves on re-renders.

options.text: Keep the grid in one `useState` 2D array and replace the whole array for each remote edit
options.why: Each of the 50 edits per second would re-render the whole grid component and its visible cells.

options.text: Virtualise rows and columns, keep cells in a store keyed by cell ID that visible cells subscribe to individually, and apply remote edits in batches once per animation frame
options.why: Only visible cells exist in the DOM, each edit wakes only its own cell, and batching caps the work at one update per frame.

options.text: Make the whole grid one `contentEditable` element and let the browser handle editing and scrolling
options.why: This removes React's control over cell state and validation, and the browser still has to lay out every cell.

explanation: Large grids need both rendering and update strategies. Rendering: virtualise in both directions so only a screenful of cells is mounted. Updates: store cells outside a single giant state value (an external store with per-cell subscriptions via `useSyncExternalStore`, or a selector-based store) and coalesce bursts of remote operations per frame. At staff level, interviewers also expect a mention of canvas rendering for very large sheets.
reference: react.dev: useSyncExternalStore; web.dev: Virtualize large lists with react-window

stem: A page has a `<SearchBar />` with a text input and a sibling `<Results />` that must filter by whatever is typed. Today `SearchBar` keeps the query in its own `useState`, so `Results` cannot see it. What is the standard React fix?

options.text: Give `Results` its own copy of the query in state, and keep the two copies in sync with a `useEffect` in each of the two components
options.why: Two copies of the same value can drift, and syncing them with effects adds extra renders and bugs.

options.text: Move the query state into their common parent, pass `query` and `onQueryChange` to `SearchBar`, and pass `query` to `Results`
options.why: The parent becomes the single source of truth, and both children get what they need through props.

options.text: Have `Results` read the input's value through a ref to the `SearchBar` input on each render
options.why: Reading a ref does not trigger a re-render, so `Results` would show stale filtering.

options.text: Store the query in a module-level variable that both components import and update
options.why: Changing a plain variable does not tell React to re-render, so `Results` would not update.

explanation: Lifting state up means moving state to the closest common ancestor of the components that need it, then passing the value down and a setter callback down. It keeps one source of truth and follows React's one-way data flow. Interviewers often follow up with "what if many levels separate them?", which leads to composition or Context.

stem: In a like-button machine-coding round, double-clicking the button sends two API requests. The button must show a loading state, must not send a second request while one is in flight, and must become clickable again even when the request fails. Which handler, used with `<button disabled={pending} onClick={handleClick}>`, meets all of that?

options.why: If the request throws, `setPending(false)` never runs, so the button stays disabled for good.
The button is disabled while the request runs, and `finally` re-enables it after both success and failure.
`useCallback` only keeps the function identity stable; it does nothing to stop a second click from sending a second request.
`pending` is set only after the request finishes, so the button is never disabled while it is in flight.

explanation: Preventing double submits means marking the action as pending before the request starts, disabling the control while it is pending, and always clearing the flag in `finally`. Interviewers use the like button to see whether you handle loading, error and success states, not just the happy path. React 19's `useActionState` and form actions provide a built-in pending state for the same purpose.
reference: react.dev: Responding to Events; MDN: try...catch (finally)

options.text: 9: the rollback uses the `count` from the click's render (10). Use `setCount(c => c - 1)` in the `catch`
options.why: The handler's `count` is a snapshot of 10, so `count - 1` is 9. A functional update subtracts from the current 11.

options.text: 10: the code is already correct, because `count` is 11 by the time the `catch` runs
options.why: State is a snapshot per render. The `count` inside this handler stays 10 even after `setCount` is called.

options.text: 11: state updates made after an `await` are ignored because they are outside the event handler
options.why: Since React 18, updates after an `await` are batched and applied normally; this one is applied, with the wrong value.

options.text: 9: fix it by writing `await setCount(count - 1)` so that the state update has finished before the next render starts
options.why: `setCount` returns nothing to wait for, and the value passed in is still computed from the stale snapshot.

explanation: Event handlers see state as it was when that render happened. Undoing an optimistic change with a value computed from that snapshot is a classic off-by-one bug. Functional updates (`c => c - 1`) apply to the latest state, so they compose correctly with any updates in between. Restoring the exact snapshot (`setCount(count)`) would also work here, but it overwrites other changes made meanwhile.
reference: react.dev: State as a Snapshot; react.dev: Queueing a Series of State Updates

stem: `Card.jsx` imports `./Card.css` and `Modal.jsx` imports `./Modal.css`. Both stylesheets define a `.title` rule with different font sizes. On pages that show both components, one component's titles take the other's size. Why, and what fixes it?

options.text: The bundler scopes each imported `.css` file to the component that imports it, so the clash must come from a stale browser cache; a hard reload fixes it
options.why: Plain CSS imports are not scoped. The rules really do conflict, and a reload will not change that.

options.text: React applies the stylesheet of whichever component renders last; rendering `Card` after `Modal` fixes it
options.why: React does not apply or order plain CSS rules per component. The order in which the bundler emits the files decides which rule wins.

options.text: The `className` prop only accepts one class, so both components should switch to inline `style` objects instead
options.why: `className` accepts any number of space-separated classes, and moving everything to inline styles loses media queries and pseudo-classes.

options.text: Imported plain CSS is global, so the two `.title` rules collide; renaming the files to `.module.css` makes each class name unique to its file
options.why: CSS Modules rewrite `.title` into a unique name per file (for example `Card_title_x1`), which removes the clash.

explanation: In React projects, importing a `.css` file adds global CSS, wherever the import is. Common ways to scope styles are CSS Modules (unique class names at build time), utility classes such as Tailwind (no custom class names to clash), and CSS-in-JS. Runtime CSS-in-JS needs a client runtime, which is why Server Component setups favour CSS Modules, Tailwind or zero-runtime libraries.

stem: You are building a `useThrottle` hook for a scroll handler. The requirement: the first scroll event runs immediately, and while scrolling continues the handler runs at most once every 200 ms. Which core `throttle` function meets the requirement?

options.why: This is a debounce: each event resets the timer, so during continuous scrolling the handler never runs at all.
Starting `last` at creation time drops the first event, so the handler does not run immediately.
`last` is updated on every event, even skipped ones, so with events every 16 ms the gap never reaches 200 ms and it fires only once.
The first call runs (the gap from 0 is large), and `last` moves only when the handler actually runs, giving one call per 200 ms.

explanation: Throttling guarantees a maximum rate; debouncing waits for a pause. A leading-edge throttle runs at once and then ignores events until the window passes. Many interviewers then ask for a trailing call (run once more with the last arguments when the window ends) so the final scroll position is not missed. Inside a hook, the throttled function must be kept stable across renders (for example in a ref or `useMemo`), with the latest handler read from a ref.
reference: MDN: Element: scroll event; MDN: Date.now()

stem: Which two of these handlers are better throttled than debounced? (Choose two.)

options.text: Updating a reading-progress bar from the page's scroll position
options.why: The bar should move smoothly while the user scrolls, so it needs regular updates during the activity, not one at the end.

options.text: Calling a search-suggestions API as the user types
options.why: Here you want to wait until typing pauses, so debouncing avoids a request for every intermediate query.

options.text: Auto-saving a draft after the user stops editing
options.why: "After the user stops" is the definition of debouncing: save once, after a quiet period.

options.text: Sending the cursor position while the user drags a shape on a shared whiteboard
options.why: Collaborators must see the shape move during the drag, so a capped rate of updates is the goal.

options.text: Validating a username for availability once the user has finished typing it
options.why: Checking after typing pauses is a debounce; throttling would send checks for half-typed names.

explanation: Use throttling when you need regular updates during continuous activity (scroll, resize while dragging, pointer moves), and debouncing when you only care about the final value after the activity stops (search, auto-save, validation). For visual updates tied to scroll or pointer movement, `requestAnimationFrame` is a natural throttle, at most once per frame.

stem: A three-step signup form renders `{step === 1 && <AccountStep />}`, `{step === 2 && <ProfileStep />}` and so on. Each step keeps its fields in its own `useState`. When the user clicks Back from step 2, the step 1 fields are empty. Which structure fixes this and keeps all the data ready for the final submit?

options.text: Add `key="account"` to `<AccountStep />` so React remembers its state between steps
options.why: A key identifies a component while it stays mounted. Once the step unmounts, its state is gone whatever its key.

options.text: Keep one `formData` object and the `step` in the parent wizard, and pass each step its values and an `onChange` that updates that object
options.why: The parent stays mounted throughout, so values survive navigation, and the final submit reads one object.

options.text: Save each step's values to `localStorage` in an effect cleanup when the step unmounts, and read them back in an effect when the step mounts again
options.why: It can work, but it adds an effect round trip and a flash of empty fields, and leaves data in storage. Lifting state is the direct fix.

options.text: Store each step's fields in a `useRef` inside the step so they are not lost on re-render
options.why: Refs also belong to the component instance and are discarded when the step unmounts.

explanation: State belongs to a component's position in the tree, and a conditionally rendered step loses its state when it unmounts. The usual fix is to lift the form data into the parent wizard (or a form library such as React Hook Form at wizard level), with the step index alongside. This also makes per-step validation and the final submit simple.

options.text: `setErrors` and `setStep` are batched into one update, so React applies `setStep` first and the new errors object is thrown away
options.why: Batching applies both updates in one render; it does not reorder or discard them. The error does appear, as the stem says.

options.text: `errors` is still this render's value (empty), so the check passes; it should check the result of `validate` directly
options.why: Calling `setErrors` does not change the `errors` variable in the running handler; it only schedules the next render.

options.text: `Object.keys` returns `undefined` for an empty object, so the length check always passes
options.why: `Object.keys({})` returns an empty array, whose length is 0; the check itself works.

options.text: `setStep(step + 1)` should be `setStep(s => s + 1)`; the stale step skips validation
options.why: A functional update helps with repeated updates, but the bug is the stale `errors` check, which a functional `setStep` does not touch.

explanation: State is a snapshot for each render. Reading state right after setting it in the same handler gives the old value. The fix is to keep the computed value in a local variable (`const next = validate(step, formData); setErrors(next); if (!Object.keys(next).length) setStep(step + 1);`). Machine-coding interviewers see this bug often in wizards and form validation.

stem: In a shopping-cart round, items are `[{ id, name, price, qty }]` in `useState`. Changing a quantity must re-render the row, and the order total must never be out of step with the items, without an extra render pass. Which implementation meets both requirements?

options.why: The array reference is unchanged, so React bails out of the update and the row does not re-render.
The update is immutable, but the total is copied into state by an effect, which costs a second render and leaves one render with the old total.
The update creates a new array with a new object for the changed item, and the total is computed from the items on every render, so it cannot drift.
Adding the new line total to the old total double-counts the item, and keeping a second copy of the total invites exactly this drift.

explanation: Two habits are being checked. First, immutable updates: map to a new array and copy the changed item, so React sees new references. Second, derived state: totals, item counts, tax and delivery fees should be computed from the items during render (wrapped in `useMemo` only if it is expensive), not stored separately and synced.
reference: react.dev: Choosing the State Structure; react.dev: Updating Arrays in State

options.text: `₹3.3 true`; floating-point errors only appear with more than two decimal places in the inputs
options.why: The input has one decimal place and still is not exact: 1.1 has no exact binary representation.

options.text: `₹3.30 true`; the fix is to call `toFixed(2)` on each price before multiplying
options.why: `toFixed` returns a string, and the template literal does not add a trailing zero. Rounding each input does not make the arithmetic exact either.

options.text: `₹3.3000000000000003 false`; keep money as integer paise (110) and format only for display
options.why: Integer arithmetic is exact, and converting to rupees with `Intl.NumberFormat` happens only when rendering.

options.text: `₹3.3000000000000003 false`; wrap the total in `Number(total.toPrecision(2))` inside the reducer
options.why: `toPrecision(2)` keeps two significant digits, so a total of 1,299.50 would become 1,300; it hides the problem and adds a bigger one.

explanation: JavaScript numbers are binary floating point, so values like 1.1 are approximations and their products pick up tiny errors. Carts usually store money in the smallest unit (paise or cents) as integers, round once when applying percentage tax, and format with `Intl.NumberFormat('en-IN', { style: 'currency', currency: 'INR' })` for display. Interviewers look for this once the cart totals work.
